book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant

chapters.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch05 - The Federation Council GEORGE A REISCH.md
ch06 - Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'

chapters.file: ch07 - Starfleet Directive ONE - Seek Out New Ideas Major Philosophical Themes in.md
ch08 - Never Underestimate a TV Writer.md
chapters.relation: Cantor argues the TNG episode 'Darmok' dramatizes Wittgenstein's later philosophy of language: Picard first reads Dathon's 'Temba, his arms wide' as naming objects — the Augustinian picture of language Wittgenstein rejects — then realizes on El-Adrel IV that Tamarian utterances mean through their use in a shared activity, as when he and Dathon fight the beast together. The Tamarians speak entirely in citations of their own myths ('Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra', 'Shaka, when the walls fell'), so language is shown to be embedded in a form of life, exactly Wittgenstein's 'if a lion could talk' problem. The chapter then ties this to E.D. Hirsch's cultural literacy — Troi's 'Juliet on her balcony' and Picard's Gilgamesh story show communication presupposes shared cultural knowledge — and concludes that the erudite writers Menosky and LaZebnik made a genuinely philosophic episode of television.

Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.

chapters.file: ch10 - “All Good Things Must Come to an End”.md
chapters.relation: Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'

Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.

chapters.file: ch12 - “Condemned to Be a Member of This Lowest of Species”.md
chapters.relation: Arp uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether unlimited power must corrupt the just: Q's career of meddling ('Encounter at Farpoint', 'Q Who?', 'The Q and the Grey') shows the corrupted case, while Riker given Q-powers in 'Hide and Q' helps his friends instead, a counterexample Glaucon can resist by pleading insufficient time. He then explains the Q's misery — Quinn's bored suicidal plea in 'Death Wish' — through the hedonistic paradox, refining it with Mill's distinction between bodily lower pleasures and mental higher ones and Aristotle's account of the lasting pleasure of completed states like beating the ship's computer at chess. The conclusion is that Q's 'condemnation' to mortality in 'Déjà Q' reveals the human condition as enviable: it is precisely our lacking unlimited power, pleasure, and immortality that drives the striving for truth, justice, goodness, and love.

chapters.file: ch13 - Starfleet Directive TWO - Go Boldly, Yet Morally Federation Ethics.md
ch14 - “Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”.md
chapters.relation: Eberl weighs genetic enhancement and cloning through Trek's test cases: Julian Bashir's parents' enhancement leaves him feeling 'a fraud' ('You used to be my father. Now, you're my architect'), the Moab IV 'Masterpiece Society' breeds out 'the unknown, self-discovery, things that make life worth living', and the Jem'Hadar show desire itself engineered for control. He argues the right to an open future constrains designing children (B'Elanna's wish to de-Klingonize her baby, Worf pressuring Alexander), defends genetic treatment while rejecting genetic determinism, and uses Kass and Rovane with Picard and Shinzon, the Mariposa clones, and Trip's clone Sim to show clones are numerically distinct persons. Against Malik's Augments quoting Nietzsche — 'mankind is something to be surpassed' — the chapter argues the Übermensch demands self-mastery through philosophy, not eugenic engineering, tracing eugenics from Plato's Guardian breeding scheme through Buck v. Bell to modern prenatal selection.

Challans argues Picard is 'Starfleet's conscience' because he exemplifies Kantian moral autonomy — acting on categorical principles like the Prime Directive rather than on orders, authority, or hypothetical imperatives — while the Borg show its total loss: assimilated drones forfeit moral agency, and the Borg Queen's pursuit of collective perfection is at best Rawls's merely 'rational autonomy.' Boétie's dupes and knaves, Nietzsche's herd, Milgram's obedience experiments, and Foucault's institutions producing docile bodies explain how war machines make complicity normal, from Gowron's corrupt Klingon Empire to Browning's 'ordinary men.' Picard passes the twenty-fourth-century Milgram tests — refusing illegal orders in 'Conundrum' and exposing 'The Pegasus', fighting Starfleet itself in Insurrection with 'How many people does it take, Admiral, before it becomes wrong?' — while the chapter closes by charging that America's real war machine now resembles the Borg more than Starfleet.

chapters.file: ch16 - “I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”.md
chapters.relation: Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.

chapters.file: ch17 - “There’s More to Life than Profit”.md
chapters.relation: Held argues business ethics stalls because it begins from capitalism's presuppositions instead of asking what we fundamentally value, staging the impasse as Quark versus Rom and as Friedman's stockholder theory against Freeman's stakeholder theory ('The Dogs of War', Zek's reforms, 'Profit and Lace'). He recovers Aristotle's Politics distinction between economics serving the household's good and chrematistics — money-making as sheer accumulation, embodied in Quark's 'pure profit' embezzlement — and corrects the libertarian caricature of Adam Smith: the invisible hand works only within commutative justice and virtue, markets serving welfare rather than profit. Through Sen's capability approach and Quark's own defense of greed as promoting human development in 'Prophet Motive', the chapter concludes profit is only a means to freedom and well-being — 'there's more to life than profit' — and the Rules of Acquisition themselves must stand before the ethical judge.

chapters.file: ch18 - Starfleet Directive THREE - A United Federation Social and Religious Values of.md
ch19 - “Obviously, the Borg Can’t Hold Their Liquor”.md
chapters.relation: Decker asks 'What's it like to be a Borg?' and tests whether monist metaphysics justify the Collective: Parmenides's changeless, perfect Being matches the Borg's 'bringing them closer to perfection', Spinoza's one substance (God or Nature) makes assimilationist determinism intelligible and finds truth in Seven of Nine's nostalgia for collective harmony, and Hegel's teleological Geist — the whole 'the world, aware of itself' — most closely mirrors the Borg's galactic quest for an Omega-molecule perfection of 'infinite parts functioning as one.' Yet 'I, Borg' shows Hegelian Spirit working through individuals: Hugh's redemption transforms the Enterprise crew's self-understanding, proving nothing is wholly alien and freedom can coexist with collectivity. Via Haraway's cyborgs and against Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance', the chapter concludes the Borg horrify us because the natural/artificial dualism is already obsolete in our technologized lives — 'if we are the Borg, then resistance truly is futile.'

holes.name: Cultural Literacy (E.D. Hirsch)
holes.what: E.D. Hirsch's thesis that reading and communication depend on shared background knowledge of a culture's vocabulary, allusions, and history rather than on content-free skills.
holes.why: Chapter 8 reads 'Darmok' as dramatizing Hirsch's claim: Picard decodes Tamarian myth-speech only through shared stories like Gilgamesh, and the episode champions Great Books.

holes.name: Classical Yoga (Patanjali's eight limbs)
holes.what: Patanjali's system of ethical restraints and observances, posture, breath control, and meditation culminating in the liberating oneness of samadhi.
holes.why: Chapter 9's core interpretive move maps Vulcan logic's three modes — formal, ethical, meditative — onto Patanjali's Yoga, reading Kolinahr and Spock's rebirth through samadhi and tantra.

holes.name: The Hedonistic Paradox
holes.what: The puzzle that pursuing pleasure for its own sake self-defeatingly yields pain, through frustration, mistaking pains for pleasures, or the boredom of getting everything wanted.
holes.why: Chapter 12 uses the paradox to explain why the omnipotent, immortal Q — Quinn in 'Death Wish' above all — end up frustrated and miserable despite unlimited power.

holes.name: Eugenics
holes.what: The program of improving the human gene pool by selective breeding or genetic intervention, historically coercive and state-driven, now debated as 'liberal eugenics'.
holes.why: Chapter 14's central cases — Khan's Augments, the Moab IV colony, prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis — are weighed against the history of eugenics from Plato to Buck v. Bell.

holes.name: The Right to an Open Future
holes.what: The principle (associated with Joel Feinberg) that parents and designers must preserve a child's future range of life choices rather than fix them in advance.
holes.why: Chapter 14 applies the concept to the Moab IV colonists, Worf and Alexander, the engineered Jem'Hadar, B'Elanna's baby, and Kass's argument against cloning.

holes.name: Milton Friedman
holes.what: Economist whose stockholder theory holds that a corporation's only social responsibility is to maximize its owners' profits within the law.
holes.why: Chapter 17 structures its business-ethics debate around Friedman's stockholder theory opposed to stakeholder theory, voiced through Quark and Grand Nagus Zek.

holes.name: Amartya Sen
holes.what: Nobel laureate economist-philosopher whose capability approach defines development as expanding the real freedoms people have reason to value, and poverty as capability deprivation.
holes.why: Chapter 17 closes by adopting Sen's capability approach to argue markets and greed are justified only as means to human welfare and freedom.

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist philosopher of science whose 'Cyborg Manifesto' argues we are already cyborgs and that natural/artificial and similar dualisms underwrite domination.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses Haraway's cyborg to dissolve the human/machine boundary the Borg violate and to reach its conclusion that 'we are the Borg'.

holes.name: Leon Kass
holes.what: Bioethicist who defends the 'wisdom of repugnance' — the view that repulsion at cloning or enhancement tracks real moral harm — and the treatment/enhancement distinction.
holes.why: Chapter 19 leans on Kass's repugnance principle to explain why the Borg disgust us, before arguing technology has already eroded that wisdom.
